conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad we’re meeting. I’m [your name], and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. My job is to help new mothers sort out the many emotions that come after a baby arrives, and one of the tools we use is the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. Everything we discuss stays between us, and there’s no judgment here—only support. I’ll read each question aloud, and you can just tell me what feels true for you. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a silly face or when the dog does something ridiculous—but it feels a little forced. I’d say… most days I manage to giggle once or twice, but I don’t feel that light, easy laughter I used to. It’s more like “okay, I’ll smile because I know this is supposed to be funny,” rather than really feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yes… but it’s not the same. I’ll laugh if my husband says something goofy or if the dog trips over his own paws, but it feels kind of hollow, like I’m going through the motions. I guess I’d say “sometimes,” because it’s not every day and it doesn’t come as naturally as it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve noticed I’m not really excited about much anymore. Like, my sister keeps asking if I want to get coffee or go for a walk, and I say yes because I know I should, but I don’t feel that little spark of “yay, something fun.” Even little outings feel like chores—pack the diaper bag, worry if the baby will cry, wonder if I’ll even enjoy myself. I guess it’s “not often” that I look forward to things right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Last night the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe it’s because my milk isn’t “good enough,” or I didn’t burp him right, or I let him get overtired. I know, logically, babies just have rough nights, but I still hear that little voice saying I should’ve handled it better. It doesn’t happen every single time something goes wrong—maybe a few times this week—but when it does, it sticks with me for a while.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days I do feel anxious, but it’s usually tied to the baby—like, is he breathing okay, is that rash normal, am I doing this right? So I guess there’s a “reason,” even if it’s probably over-the-top. I can’t say I’ve been worried for no good reason, but the worry still feels constant and hard to turn off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really “no good reason.” I’ve had a couple moments where my heart races—usually if the baby starts coughing or if I wake up and the monitor’s gone quiet—but it feels tied to him, not out of nowhere. I haven’t had that sudden, unexplainable panic, so I’d say “no, not much.”
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… there are definitely times when it all feels like too much. The diapers, the feedings, the laundry, trying to squeeze in a shower—some days it just piles up and I think, “How is everyone else doing this?” I’m not falling apart, but a few times this week I’ve had to set the baby in the crib for five minutes, walk to the kitchen, and just breathe so I don’t cry. I’d say “yes, sometimes” things feel like they’re getting on top of me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t call it “so unhappy,” but I have been lying awake some nights. My mind just keeps running through the next day—how many ounces he drank, whether the diaper rash is better, if I’ll manage to nap at all. Once I’m up for a feeding it can take me an hour to drift off again. So yes, I’ve had trouble sleeping several nights this week, though it feels more like busy-brain than pure unhappiness.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like a little cloud that follows me around—but it’s not every moment. Yesterday I teared up while folding onesies for no clear reason, and I’ve had that heavy feeling off and on through the week. I’d say “yes, sometimes,” because it’s there, just not all day long.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I’ve gotten teary a couple of times—like when the baby wouldn’t settle and I felt useless—but I haven’t sat there sobbing or felt so unhappy that crying just took over. Maybe once or twice a few tears slipped out, but that’s about it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 4–6 wks post-delivery, breastfeeding, husband/support present.

Self-report on Edinburgh scale items:

1. Anhedonia / low mood  
   – Diminished enjoyment of previously pleasurable activities (“hollow” laughter, outings feel like chores).  
   – Endorses “sometimes” sad/miserable, teary without clear trigger (Q8).  

2. Anxiety, worry, hyper-arousal  
   – Near-daily, infant-focused worries; sleep latency after night feeds; heart racing with minor infant cues (Q4, Q5, Q7).  

3. Self-blame / guilt  
   – Intermittent, situation-specific guilt re feeding/soothing adequacy; ruminates after fussy episodes (Q3).

4. Feeling overwhelmed  
   – Endorses “sometimes” unable to keep up with daily baby-care tasks; uses brief “time-outs” to prevent tearfulness (Q6).

5. Sleep disturbance  
   – Trouble returning to sleep after night feeds 3–4 nights/week; linked to racing thoughts rather than solely infant demands (Q7).

6. Crying  
   – Occasional tears (Q9), denies frank crying spells.

7. Safety  
   – Denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10). No current safety concern.

Summary: Sub-threshold but clinically significant mixed depressive and anxiety symptoms. Enjoyment reduction, intermittent sadness and guilt, persistent infant-focused worry, and mild sleep impairment present; no self-harm ideation. Continue monitoring, consider formal EPDS scoring, and evaluate functional impairment at follow-up visit.
